explanation: Fires on the second or third token of a fixed multi-token term or name, where the earlier tokens make the rest predictable: 'electroph[ores]is', 'esc[_html]', 'fly[weight]', 'DataSt[ax]', 'Royal Astronomical [Society]', 'Anders v. California', 'get a [warrant]', 'Unless stated [otherwise]'. Content-wise the hits are unrelated (science, code, law), so I can't see one concept; the shared thread looks like 'completing a predictable collocation'.

Fires on a tech company, platform or brand name, or the word right before it, in a context that names a product or vendor: 'the [OnePlus] 5', 'for [Windows] 10', 'Copyright 2016 [The] Go/Chromium Authors', '[Apple] Inc.', 'Epic', 'Sony', 'LG', 'Lotus'. Weaker on other proper nouns such as countries or sports teams.

Fires on the first sub-token of a word split into pieces, especially a word-initial fragment like ' cr' (cranked, criminologist, crashing, craves, crummy), 'y' (y'know, yesterday, yodeling), 'O'(xford), '(c)', 'x'(86), and on the first digit of a multi-digit number in a date or time ('at [1]1.20', 'on [1]2 July', '1[0]:18'). Roughly: the start of a token sequence that will be continued.

Fires in casual, conversational or narrative English (dialogue, song titles, blog first person) on a word in the middle of an idiom or clause, especially 'I' right after an interjection or quote ('Oh, [I] love this', '"[I] do not understand'), and on idiom pieces ('at the [last] second', 'can't [wait]', 'jump on the scene', 'came across', 'I'm [late]'). Weak in formal or technical text.

Fires in source code on a variable or identifier used as an operand on the right-hand side of an assignment or inside an expression or argument, especially when that variable was just defined or assigned ('string = [string].replace', 'output = [output] +', 'this.Name = [name]', 'return [res]', 'type[_table]:split'), and on closing parens that end such expressions. Weak in non-code text.

No clear common feature. It fires on word-piece fragments in non-English text (Czech 'sam', French 'veulent', 'et', 'ass'), on fragments of proper names (Ceb-al-los, Mon-ash, G-ugg-enheim, J-ef-te), on whitespace and indentation in build files and legal headers, and on some ordinary English verbs ('take', 'come'). Maybe a mixture tied to unusual tokenisation.

Fires strongly on the decimal point inside software version numbers ('Maven 3[.]6.3', 'LLVM 2[.]9', 'License-2[.]0', 'Version 2[.]0') and also on function words or mid-word pieces in non-English text (French 'sachant', 'en'; Russian 'не', '-ается'). It also gets some English idiom pieces ('can't', 'all time high').

Fires on the head noun of a formal definite noun phrase that a following clause or definition is about to explain, most of all 'invention' in patent boilerplate 'The present [invention] relates to', and also 'Policy', 'motto', 'word', and on 'that' opening a relative clause ('the forum [that] you want'). It marks a noun that is about to be specified.

Fires on the second half of a contrast or comparison, the word that gives the contrasting outcome or direction: 'hypoactivation... and hyper[activation]', 'exclude... but must [include]', 'whereas [decrease]', 'did [not] inhibit', 'not [guilty]', 'the [loss]', 'got [worse]', '[0] to remove'. Common in scientific results and legal holdings.

Mixed. In LaTeX math it fires on variable or set symbols inside expressions ('(X', 'F^A', '-Uv', ':X'); in code on generic or type brackets and members ('Set<T', 'and_<', '.allows'); and in English on light-verb idioms with 'give'/'it' ('I'll [give] you', 'giving [it] praises', 'give it a shot', 'doesn't make sense'). These don't share an obvious concept.

Fires on the first sub-token or stem of a multi-token word, often a verb, whose ending comes next ('asc-ends', 'iss-us', 'beck-ons', 'occ-uring', 'prev-ails', 'enc-odes', 'lip-oprotein', 'Secret-ariat'), and on mid-sentence verb stems in Japanese text. It also fires on some nouns in set phrases ('the [face] and voice', 'Palace of').

Fires on the adverb suffix token '-ly' (and '-ively', '-ately', '-ously', '-ically', Portuguese '-amente') when it is a separate sub-token added to an adjective stem ('benign[ly]', 'seduct[ively]', 'nast[ily]'). Whole-word adverbs ('reasonably', 'commonly', 'shortly') get only moderate activation.

Fires on the preposition 'of' or 'to' that follows a nominalised noun taking a complement: 'The presence [of]', 'capability [to]/[of]', 'access [to]', 'wealth of', 'President of', 'Remember to', 'entitled to'. 'The presence of' is the strongest pattern. Weak on other function words.

Mostly fires on 'mobile' as a modifier (mobile device, mobile telephone, 'mobile-first', fixed or mobile). It also fires on a scattered set of other modifiers and prefixes ('mid-1970s', 'Marvel', 'non-smoker', 'rebel-controlled', 'multiple', 'DNA meth-'). 'mobile' is the clear main job; the rest look like loosely related compound-modifier positions.

No single pattern. It fires on statistics notation ('SD[=]', 'mean [age]'), on nouns after a determiner or adjective ('GE's [motion]', 'Series B [round]', 'A [source]', 'video [conclusion]'), on code and math fragments ('sp[lice]', 'dy[dt]', 'z[**]', 'SQL[STATE]'), and on random digits in timestamps or citations.

Fires in source code at the start of a declaration or statement: the return type after an access modifier ('public [int]', 'public static [void]'), 'import' in 'from x import', 'function' or 'def' starting a definition, 'super', and an exception variable at the start of a statement ('[e].printStackTrace'). Weak inside expressions and in prose.

Fires on the token 'de' / 'De' / 'DE' as the start of a word (de-lectable, de-amon, De-puties, de-oxyribo, De-borah, de-bate) or as a particle in names ('de Tocqueville', 'de Kooning', 'de la Cruz'). It is weaker for related prefixes such as 'di', 'dec', 'Dem' and for 'de' inside a word.

Fires on a middle sub-token of a word split into several pieces, mostly a vowel-rich fragment inside a longer or rarer word (kallik-re-in, Mujah-ide-en, counter-fe-iting, fort-ale-cer, HOMEST-E-ADER, child-re-aring, displ-easure), in many languages. Activation is moderate overall (one 100% outlier, Estonian 'surve').

No coherent pattern. It fires on file-name and URL fragments ('.min', '.component', '/*.'), on hex or ID digits, on punctuation inside data ('%),'), and on scattered English words ('airway', 'suggested', 'where', 'pleasure').

Unclear. It fires on the second item of a pair or on the start of an abbreviation ('dest1, dest2', '#section1 [and]', '[PD]GF', 'AD and [ps]oriasis', '[FG]Fs', '[eos]inophil'), on commas after introductory phrases, and on assorted nouns ('decision', 'control', 'items'). There is no clear shared trigger.

Fires on the last digit of a four-digit year that is written as split tokens ('200[7]', '201[0]') in a full date that follows a month and day ('March 27, 200[7]', '12 March 197[2]'). Strongest for 2000s/2010s years; weaker for older years and when the year is a single token after a space.
